original_question: Does the presence of an axillary lymph node measuring 13 mm without a fatty hilum suggest T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia?
key_entities: fatty hilum suggest T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia

final_qi.question: Does the presence of an axillary lymph node measuring 13 mm without a fatty hilum suggest T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia?
final_qi.long_answer: A 13-mm axillary lymph node lacking a fatty hilum is radiologically suspicious for malignancy, but it is a non-specific finding. Many conditions—reactive hyperplasia, metastatic solid tumors, B-cell or T-cell lymphomas, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and other leukemias—can produce enlarged nodes without a fatty hilum. T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) is a rare mature T-cell leukemia diagnosed primarily by marked peripheral blood lymphocytosis, characteristic cytomorphology, immunophenotyping, and specific chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., inv(14)(q11q32), t(14;14)). Imaging findings such as a single mildly enlarged axillary node are neither sensitive nor specific for T-PLL. Therefore, the mere presence of a 13-mm axillary lymph node without a fatty hilum does not, by itself, suggest T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.

final_qi.question: What is the significance of an axillary lymph node measuring 13 mm without a fatty hilum in relation to T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia?
final_qi.long_answer: A 13-mm axillary node that has lost its normal fatty hilum is considered pathologic; in a patient with T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia this finding most commonly signifies leukemic (malignant) infiltration of the lymph node, reflecting active disease or progression.
